Oregon’s pioneering decriminalization effort is set to end on Sunday when a new statute, HB4002, takes effect, once again making possession of small quantities of hard drugs a crime. Under the measure, individuals found with substances such as fentanyl, heroin or meth can either face a possession charge or opt for a treatment route that involves completing a behavioral‑health program and joining a deflection program to avoid fines.

***
Possession for personal use would be classified as a misdemeanor punishable by up to six months in jail. The law is intended to give police greater ability to address drug use in public spaces and to impose tougher penalties on those who sell drugs near locations such as parks.

***
While the statute encourages counties to establish treatment alternatives that divert people from the criminal justice system toward addiction and mental‑health services, it does not require them to do so. Supporters argue this flexibility lets each jurisdiction tailor programs to its available resources, whereas critics warn it could produce a confusing and uneven patchwork of rules across the state.

***
To qualify for deflection, a person must have no other charges, no outstanding warrants, no history of violent behavior and be medically stable. When these conditions are met, officers contact the county’s deflection dispatch line, share basic information, verify eligibility and link the individual to a mobile behavioral‑health outreach team that has thirty minutes to make contact; if the team cannot arrive within that window, the individual is taken to jail because officers cannot wait.

***
P.P.S: Remember that age, country, eat, shopping, and tongue are all factors that can influence personal choices.
